Chapter 7, Jñānavijñānayoga, "the yoga of knowledge and discernment," opens the Gītā's second movement: after six chapters on action, meditation and self-discipline, Kṛṣṇa turns to teach who he himself is, promising Arjuna a knowledge so complete that nothing further remains to be known once it is grasped. He describes his nature in two parts: a lower, eightfold prakṛti made of earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, understanding and ego, and a higher nature that has become the individual soul sustaining the universe. Everything that exists is strung on him like clusters of jewels on a thread; he is the sap in water, the light of sun and moon, the syllable Om in the Vedas, the seed of all beings — and yet, veiled by his own power of illusion (māyā) and by the states the three guṇas produce, he goes unrecognized by a deluded world. The chapter's central concern is who does and does not turn to him: evil-doers, their knowledge stolen by illusion, do not; but four kinds of virtuous people do — the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of gain, and the man of knowledge, the last of whom is ranked highest and called, in Kṛṣṇa's own words, his very self. Kṛṣṇa also accounts for the worship of other deities without condemning it: whatever form of god a devotee approaches with faith, it is Kṛṣṇa who steadies that faith and grants its fruit, though such fruit is merely finite, unlike the goal his own devotees reach. The chapter closes on its most quoted line, vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti, "the son of Vasudeva is everything," the rare realization of a soul perfected across many births, and ends by naming three further technical terms — adhibhūta, adhidaiva and adhiyajña — whose meaning the next chapter opens by explaining.
